title: President to unveil investment-oriented 2027 Budget today, with relief for masses | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:00
-     - 191

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake (right) with Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma reviewing the finalised 2027 Budget proposals yesterday

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake is expected to present an investment-oriented 2027 Budget in Parliament today, with some relief for masses impacted by the tough stabilisation measures of the past two years, climate change and the Middle East conflict.

As hinted by the President and his Ministers in recent weeks, the Pay As You Earn threshold is set to be adjusted upwards again and no new taxes or rate increases are expected, as the Government squares pre-announced relief with International Monetary Fund (IMF) conditions for a $ 345 million tranche and El Niño and the Middle East war that are eroding growth assumptions.

The Budget, the Government’s third, carries Rs. 4.99 trillion in service expenditure and a Rs. 3.8 trillion net borrowing cap.

Relief is to be delivered in stages. The President has told a trade union convention that the PAYE threshold, already raised from Rs. 100,000 to Rs. 150,000, will be adjusted again, and has set out a two to three year VAT reduction alongside a one-year deferral of the IMF-backed property tax. No new taxes or rate increases are expected, with the revenue strategy resting on compliance rather than rate changes.

Revenue mobilisation is running well ahead of targets. The original target was to raise Government revenue to 15.4% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by 2030, but the country had already exceeded 16% by end-2025. This year’s target, set under ceilings referenced to the Public Financial Management Act, has been kept at around 15% and is comfortably within reach.

Once that level is secured, space opens to fund much-needed public investment and to consider strategies to reset the present tax structure. Problems in corporate income tax and individual income tax are acknowledged, but rates are unlikely to come down at this stage without delaying revenue mobilisation. A reduction in indirect taxation becomes possible once revenue reaches the required level, with all tax policy changes to be guided by fairness, simplicity and convenience.

The Budget carries Rs. 2 trillion in capital allocations, prioritising roads, railways, rural connectivity and networks, logistics, and some social spending, and is framed as a move beyond the goal of economic stabilisation towards economic expansion and transformative development. The President reviewed the final document at the Presidential Secretariat on 11 November. Existing bureaucratic systems and resources, however, constrain the State’s ability to spend at speed, and discussions on accelerating disbursement are already under way.

Most macroeconomic stabilisation targets have been met ahead of or within the expected timeframe, drawing recognition from local stakeholders, diplomatic missions, international agencies and independent rating agencies. The stated task now is to move past stabilisation into real transformation, with investment needed both local and foreign, Finance Deputy Minister Anil Jayantha Fernando recently said.

Domestic savings are identified as the immediate opportunity, given the gap between savings and investment, with the capital market cast as the channel for pooling scattered savings and directing them into the real economy. To that end, capital market policies are to be far more visible in the 2027 Budget, with an acknowledgement that steps taken over the past two years were not widely seen and led some to conclude little had been done for the market, Fernando said.

Most of the 12 capital market development proposals submitted by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka (SEC) have already been discussed and accepted by the Finance Ministry. Some will be included in the Budget proposals, while the remainder will be discussed further and implemented in consultation with the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) and the SEC. Required legal amendments are to be introduced, with new Acts in the pipeline for presentation to Parliament, and the single window project for investment facilitation through technology is nearing completion.

The Appropriation Bill, Gazetted on 18 September, 2026 by order of the President as Finance Minister, sets service expenditure for Ministries and Departments at Rs. 4.99 trillion and statutory expenditure, charged to the Consolidated Fund by other laws, at Rs. 4.92 trillion, for total expenditure of about Rs. 9.92 trillion. Net outstanding Government borrowings are capped at no more than Rs. 3.8 trillion for the year.

The structure shows how far recurrent commitments constrain the Budget. The Department of Pensions alone accounts for Rs. 550.35 billion of the Public Administration Ministry’s Rs. 651 billion. Provincial Councils are budgeted separately at Rs. 574.95 billion recurrent and Rs. 85 billion capital, a combined Rs. 659.95 billion, taking the Ministry’s effective allocation to about Rs. 1.31 trillion, ahead of Finance.

The IMF reached staff-level agreement on the Seventh Review of the $ 3 billion Extended Fund Facility on 8 November, making Executive Board approval contingent on the Budget being presented in line with program parameters and on adequate progress with debt restructuring. The arrangement ends in March 2027, with debt service stepping up in 2028. Revenue must stay above 15.3% and 15.4% of GDP in 2026 and 2027, with primary expenditure capped at 12.9% of GDP. The Government has told the Fund that Budget revenue measures will suffice for targets.

The external backdrop has worsened. The IMF said the economy grew 4.2% in the second quarter, an eleventh consecutive quarter of expansion, with reserves at $ 6.9 billion at end-August, but flagged risks from the war’s duration and intensity, global trade policy and El Niño. “Safeguarding macroeconomic stability in a shock-prone environment requires continuing with prudent policies and bold reforms to protect the hard-won gains of the program,” it said, pressing for fuel prices to track global markets.

Inflation rose to 8.3% year-on-year in October from 8% in September, a three-year high. The current account swung to a $ 128 million deficit in September, taking the nine-month shortfall to $ 420 million against a $ 1.9 billion surplus a year earlier. Equity outflows reached $ 170.2 million over the nine months, against $ 85 million a year before, though direct investment in the balance of payments primary account exceeded $ 1 billion, up from $ 841 million.

Analysts point out that the economy is undergoing its most fundamental change in seven to eight decades. Twin fiscal and current account surpluses were last recorded in the 1950s and the shift will reward capital-intensive, margin-driven businesses while squeezing labour-intensive, volume-based players, as the Government avoids loose fiscal policy in a break from the past. However, the fiscal gains and economic stabilisation have been uneven, not benefiting vulnerable groups.

Other analysts argue that the fiscal responsibility framework must survive the Budget. They want revenue to increase through a widened tax net, and call for a healthy primary surplus, a contained deficit and a shift from recurrent to capital spending through procurement changes, with tax moderated rather than cut. Policy stability mattered more than any single Budget.

Advocate Institute has called for an independent Tax Ombudsman with binding timelines, noting that of Rs. 2.16 trillion in arrears at end-2025, Rs. 1.68 trillion is disputed and interest on disputed balances rose from Rs. 81 billion to Rs. 278 billion in a year. They want Port City residential exemptions of up to 25 years abolished, given apartments there sell at about $ 500 a square foot to roughly 6,000 families, and an end to property tax breaks for the Port City casino.

They also seek an end to lotteries as a revenue tool, parity between online gaming and casinos, and a financially independent Gambling Regulatory Authority. On food, they calculate that taxes make up Rs. 308 of the retail price of chicken and want the Rs. 50 per kilo Special Commodity Levy on imported corn replaced with VAT, import quotas ended and cash transfers used to support about 35,000 registered maize farmers. On paddy, they want Bim Saviya titling accelerated, since freehold deeds for nearly two million families would otherwise take about 100 years, and the Plant Variety Protection Act passed.

The Second Reading vote is set for 6 p.m. on 20 November and the Third Reading for 14 December.

title: Govt. says 2027 Budget to focus on economic transformation | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:26

Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando

Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando yesterday described the 2027 Budget, to be presented today by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, as a long-term economic transformation plan aimed at moving Sri Lanka towards upper-middle-income status.

He said the Budget would set out a phased pathway, supported by strategies, specific actions and priority-based resource allocations, to take the country beyond economic stabilisation towards sustained transformation.

In a special statement, Dr. Fernando said the Budget should be assessed holistically rather than through allocations to individual ministries and expenditure vote lines. He described the first two Budgets as having focused on establishing macroeconomic stability, which he said had now been achieved.

“The focus now needs to shift from stabilisation towards transformation,” he said, identifying quality investment, broader economic participation, job creation, higher productivity and increased production for export markets as key priorities.

He said the 2027 Budget had been structured around these priorities, with fiscal discipline remaining central, and stressed that there would be no room for corruption or waste.

While acknowledging that targeted groups would receive welfare support and tax concessions, Dr. Fernando urged the public to look beyond individual benefits when assessing the Budget.

“We should not look only at welfare benefits or tax concessions, but consider the overall macroeconomic policy direction of the Budget,” he said.

title: Gardiner Group acquires The Pickle Island in strategic leisure expansion | Daily FT
summary:

From left: The Pickle Island Founders Dilshan and Ronali Michael along with investors Aravinda de Silva, Sanjeev Gardiner and Gardiner Group Director, Investments and M&A Seshaan Gardiner

The Gardiner Group has acquired The Pickle Island, a Sri Lankan pickleball venture focused on developing the sport and its growing community, marking its entry into the country’s emerging sports and recreational leisure market. 

With seasoned investor and entrepreneur Aravinda de Silva joining as a partner, the acquisition represents the first step in what the Group describes as a broader investment strategy to build a portfolio of diversified leisure businesses in Sri Lanka.

Gardiner Group is a Sri Lankan hospitality and investment group with a longstanding legacy in the country’s hospitality industry. Its portfolio includes the iconic Galle Face Hotel, established in 1864; Ceylon Hotels Corporation PLC, with its portfolio of hotels and resthouses; and The Kandy Hotels Company (1938) PLC, which owns the historic Queen’s Hotel and Hotel Suisse in Kandy.

The Group also holds 50:50 joint venture interests in Uga Giri Ella and Radisson Hotel Kandy.

Building on this established hospitality heritage, Gardiner Group is expanding its business interests into complementary areas of leisure, lifestyle and experiences, reinforcing its long-term commitment to Sri Lanka’s hospitality and leisure sectors.

Gardiner Group Director, Investments and M&A Seshaan Gardiner said: “Our heritage is in hospitality, but our vision extends well beyond the traditional hotel experience, as we see significant opportunities to invest in Sri Lanka’s evolving leisure and lifestyle landscape. The Pickle Island represents one of several strategic investments we intend to make as we expand into new sectors, create meaningful experiences, and build on our long term confidence in Sri Lanka’s potential, both for those who call it home and those who visit.”

Founded by Ronali and Dilshan Michael, The Pickle Island was created to give people a healthy and enjoyable outlet to socialise, connect and engage through sport. It has since helped build a growing community around pickleball in Sri Lanka.

The new partnership will support its next phase of growth through wider access, new opportunities, sporting related social events, and community-focused initiatives. Ronali and Dilshan will remain closely involved, helping preserve the identity and ethos on which the business has been built.

Aravinda de Silva said: “Sport has the ability to bring people together. I look forward to supporting The Pickle Island as it continues to grow and create more opportunities for people to participate.”

This investment marks a significant step in Gardiner Group’s broader strategy to expand its presence in Sri Lanka’s leisure sector. Building on its established hospitality portfolio, the Group is pursuing new opportunities across leisure and lifestyle, with a focus on creating experiences that appeal to both Sri Lankans and international visitors.

title: Dialog maintains growth momentum in 3Q | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:22
-     - 39

Dialog Axiata PLC yesterday said it posted a group revenue of Rs. 144 billion for the first nine-months of 2026, representing a year-to-date (YTD) growth of 8% underpinned by robust performance across the mobile, fixed and digital pay television businesses.

On a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) and year-on-year (YoY) basis, group revenue grew 1% and 6% respectively to Rs. 48.5 billion in 3Q 2026, supported by growth in data and home broadband revenues. 

Group Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation (EBITDA) grew 20% YTD to Rs. 75.8 billion, supported by strong revenue growth and continued operational efficiencies. The Group EBITDA margin expanded by 5.4 percentage points (pp) compared to the first nine months of 2025, supported by continued efficiency gains. For 3Q 2026, group EBITDA was recorded at Rs. 25.9 billion, up 1% QoQ and 15% YoY.

Group Net Profit After Tax (NPAT) grew 92% YTD to Rs. 28.5 billion for the first nine months of 2026, supported by strong EBITDA growth and lower net finance cost. 3Q 2026 NPAT reached Rs. 9.2 billion, representing a 62% YoY increase despite declining 9% QoQ. Excluding unrealised forex losses, underlying NPAT increased to Rs. 10.2 billion for the quarter, growing 6% QoQ and 67% YoY and demonstrating continued strength in underlying earnings. On the same basis, NPAT for the first nine months of 2026 reached Rs. 28.9 billion, recording 82% YTD growth. 

Supported by strong operational performance, the group recorded Operating Free Cash Flow (OFCF) of Rs. 30.5 billion for the first nine months of 2026. 

Following a review of the group’s financial performance and future investment requirements, the Board of Directors of Dialog Axiata PLC approved a third interim dividend of 70 cents per share for FY 2026 at its meeting held on 10 November 2026. This brings the YTD dividend distribution to Rs. 2.10 per share and represents an annualised dividend yield of 6.2%, based on the company’s closing share price for 3Q 2026. The dividend reflects Dialog’s continued commitment to delivering sustainable shareholder returns while supporting long-term growth investments. 

Dialog Group remained a key contributor to State revenue, remitting a total of Rs. 45.1 billion to the Government of Sri Lanka (GoSL) YTD 2026. This comprised Rs. 10.9 billion in direct taxes and levies and Rs. 34.2 billion in indirect taxes collected on behalf of the GoSL. On a YTD basis, total taxes paid increased by 8%, with direct taxes up 17% and indirect taxes up 5%. 

Group capital expenditure for the first nine months of 2026 amounted to Rs. 27.4 billion, resulting in a capex-to-revenue ratio of 19%. Investments were primarily directed towards the accelerated rollout of next generation infrastructure with more than 220 new sites added during the period expanding the overall network footprint to approximately 5,700 sites nationwide, including over 1,050 live 5G sites across all 25 districts. The investment also supports greater customer adoption of advanced technologies, strengthens Dialog’s readiness to meet rapidly growing data demand and positions the Group to capture future digital growth opportunities. 

At an entity (company) level, Dialog Axiata PLC continued to be the primary contributor to group revenue (77%) and group EBITDA (74%). 

Underpinned by YoY growth in the data segment and continued operational efficiencies, company revenue grew 10% YTD to Rs. 110.9 billion, while EBITDA increased 20% YTD to Rs. 56 billion for the first nine months of 2026. On a YoY basis, company revenue grew 7%, while EBITDA increased 9%, reflecting flow-through gains from revenue growth and continued cost efficiencies. 

Company NPAT grew 94% YTD to Rs. 22.2 billion, while 3Q 2026 NPAT increased 41% YoY to Rs. 6.4 billion, primarily due to lower net finance cost, partly offset by unrealised forex losses. Excluding the unrealised forex impact, NPAT grew 83% YTD to Rs. 22.9 billion, while 3Q 2026 NPAT increased 50% YoY to Rs. 7.2 billion. 

Dialog Television (DTV) maintained its leadership in the Pay-TV sector with a subscriber base of over 1.6 million as at end-September 2026. YTD revenue grew 13% to reach Rs. 11 billion, reflecting strong growth in advertising revenue. The top line growth translated to strong EBITDA performance of 57% YTD to reach Rs. 3.1 billion for the first nine months of 2026. Accordingly, DTV recorded a YTD NPAT of Rs. 0.4 billion. 

Dialog Broadband Networks (DBN) featuring the group’s fixed telecommunications, broadband and international businesses recorded YTD revenue of Rs. 27.3 billion, reflecting a growth of 6% YTD, driven by fixed broadband revenue. DBN’s EBITDA grew 16% YTD to reach Rs. 16.5 billion for the first nine months of 2026, with EBITDA margin expanding to 60%, up 5.2pp compared to the first nine months of 2025. NPAT was recorded at Rs. 6.1 billion for the first nine months of 2026, up 46% YTD driven by EBITDA growth, lower depreciation and net finance cost.

Jeewantha said: “We decided to join the 12th Annual Cyber Security Summit as the Official Banking Partner because cybersecurity is a strategic priority for the bank and a fundamental pillar of customer trust. title: Thailand allows alcohol sales at five types of venues on Buddhist holidays | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:20
-     - 54

BANGKOK: Thailand has revised its alcohol regulations to allow sales at five categories of venues on major Buddhist religious holidays, while maintaining the general prohibition at other establishments.

The notification, issued by the Alcoholic Beverage Control Committee, was published in the Royal Gazette on 6 November and took effect on 7 November.

The new rules replace the Prime Minister’s Office notification dated 7 May 2025, with the committee stating that the regulations needed to be updated to reflect changing circumstances.

Under the notification, alcohol sales remain prohibited on five major Buddhist holidays: Makha Bucha Day, Visakha Bucha Day, Asalha Bucha Day, the beginning of Buddhist Lent and the end of Buddhist Lent.

The exemptions cover buildings serving passengers at airports operating international flights, licenced entertainment venues operating under the relevant legislation, and hotels recognised under Thai hotel law.

They also apply to establishments operating in a manner similar to entertainment venues in tourist areas, provided these are designated by the Minister of Public Health on the recommendation of the Minister of the Interior.

The fifth exemption covers venues hosting major national or international special events attended by large numbers of people. Eligible locations must be included in a list announced by the Minister of Public Health on the recommendation of the Minister of Tourism and Sports.

They must also implement safeguards to restrict access to alcoholic beverages among children and young people.

The notification was issued under Sections 16(3) and 28, paragraph one, of the Alcoholic Beverage Control Act 2008, as amended by the Alcoholic Beverage Control Act (No. 2) 2025.

The regulations follow a resolution adopted by the Alcoholic Beverage Control Committee at its second meeting of 2026, held on 17 April.

The revised notification maintains the five designated Buddhist holidays as alcohol-free sales days for establishments outside the specified exemptions, while allowing eligible venues to continue selling alcoholic beverages under the conditions set by law. - The Nation/ANN

Haycarb PLC, has delivered a strong financial performance for the six months ending 30 September 2026, recording revenue of Rs. 40.6 billion, up 42% year-on-year, while profit before tax increased 75% to Rs. 4.0 billion. Attributable Profit to shareholders grew 98% to Rs. 2.5 billion, with earnings per share increasing to Rs. 8.41.

The Group strengthened its position in gold recovery and water treatment applications through increased market penetration and product development initiatives, diversifying its revenue base and supporting margin enhancement. A key contributor to growth during the period was the continued expansion of Haycarb’s energy storage carbon portfolio, where global demand for specialized activated carbons used in advanced energy storage applications remains robust.

Haycarb PLC Chairman and its parent company Hayleys PLC Chairman Mohan Pandithage said: “The Group’s performance reflects the continued successful execution of its transformation strategy, focused on expanding its portfolio of value-added activated carbon solutions, market growth, strengthening its global manufacturing footprint, and enhancing resilience across its supply chain within the ESG framework.”

The period was also characterised by significant volatility in coconut shell charcoal availability and pricing across several sourcing markets. Amid these challenges, Haycarb’s established sourcing and manufacturing ecosystem of extensive supplier network, diversified raw material sourcing model, and geographically distributed manufacturing operations served as a strategic competitive advantage and enabled the Group to maintain continuity of supply and support customer requirements across key global markets.

To support growing demand and mitigate supply-side risks amid geopolitical tensions and extreme climate impacts, Haycarb strategically increased raw material and finished goods inventory holdings during the period, which enabled the Group to maintain production stability and customer service levels. Trade receivables also increased in line with business growth, reflecting the higher revenue base achieved during the period.

Haycarb PLC Managing Director Rajitha Kariyawasan said: “The Company continued to advance several strategic growth initiatives during the period as part of its long-term value creation agenda. Capital expenditure amounted to Rs. 4.8 billion at Group level during the six months under review, of which Rs. 3 billion was invested by the Sri Lankan operations. These investments mainly support ongoing capacity expansion of higher-value activated carbon products for energy storage applications in Sri Lanka and deployment of the strategic initiative of a greenfield manufacturing location in Philippines.”

The increase in capital employed is aligned with the Group’s ongoing capital expansion programme and commitment to building long-term capacity and market leadership in value added product segments, supply chain resilience, and future earnings potential.

Looking ahead, Haycarb remains well positioned to capitalise on growing global demand for sustainable purification, gold recovery, and energy storage solutions. Backed by its global manufacturing footprint, strong sourcing network and continued investment in sustainable innovation and value addition, the Group remains confident in its ability to deliver long-term growth while advancing its transformation into a leading provider of specialised activated carbon solutions worldwide.

title: WindForce posts strong 1H growth, accelerates renewable energy expansion | Daily FT

WindForce PLC recorded solid financial growth during the first half of FY2026/27, while advancing major solar, wind and battery energy storage investments that will significantly expand its renewable energy portfolio.

Consolidated revenue for the six months ended 30 September 2026 increased to Rs. 5.61 billion from Rs. 4.68 billion a year earlier. Gross profit rose to Rs. 3.21 billion, while profit after tax reached Rs. 1.86 billion, compared with Rs. 1.77 billion in the corresponding period. The receipt of the first $ 5 million tranche of the company’s $ 18 million facility with the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, further strengthened access to long-term international capital.

These results were delivered despite renewable energy curtailments that caused an estimated Rs. 193.57 million in foregone revenue during the period. Although the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka has approved a compensation methodology and directed the National System Operator to compensate generators based on applicable energy purchase tariffs, discussions remain ongoing and the timing and recovery of compensation are uncertain.

In September 2026, the 100 MW Rividhanavi Solar Park at Siyambalanduwa achieved financial closure, securing Rs. 22.736 billion and the rupee equivalent of $ 33 million in syndicated term loan and bank guarantee facilities. The consortium was led by Sampath Bank PLC, with Commercial Bank of Ceylon PLC, National Development Bank PLC and Nations Trust Bank PLC, enabling the project to progress into construction.

The Company also commissioned the 5 MW Diya Janani floating solar project at Dambulu Oya Reservoir in September. As one of Sri Lanka’s pioneering private-sector floating solar developments, the project demonstrates WindForce’s commitment to innovative, land-efficient renewable energy solutions.

WindForce commissioned its 10 MW/40 MWh Anuradhapura Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in September, the first completed facility in a portfolio of 13 standalone projects totalling 130 MW/520 MWh under Sri Lanka’s first grid-scale BESS initiative. Four additional facilities—in Mahiyanganaya, Ampara, Panadura and Vavuniya—were commissioned in October, adding 40 MW/160 MWh and bringing the operational total to five facilities.

The portfolio represents an investment exceeding Rs. 22.5 billion and is being developed under a 15-year Build, Own and Operate model. Once completed, these projects are expected to enhance grid stability, support renewable energy integration and reduce pressure on the national grid during peak evening demand.

Beyond these milestones, WindForce continues to advance a development pipeline exceeding 240 MW. This includes the proposed 50 MW Mullikulam Wind Power Project through Aeroforce (Pvt) Ltd and a 10 MW wind project through Safe Power International Ltd., reinforcing the Company’s focus on a diversified generation mix and Sri Lanka’s long-term energy security.

Managing Director Manjula Perera said: “Over the past 16 years, WindForce has built a strong renewable energy platform. Our ambition now is to double the capacity we have built over those 16 years within the next three years. With major projects moving through construction and commissioning, and stronger access to international financing, we are well positioned for the next phase of growth.”

title: Aberdeen Group announces leadership transition at Ex-pack Corrugated Cartons PLC: Sattar Kassim retires as Chairman, Thulci Aluwihare appointed | Daily FT

Sattar Kassim (left) and Thulci Aluwihare

Aberdeen Group announced that Sattar Kassim will retire from the Board of its listed subsidiary, Ex-pack Corrugated Cartons PLC, with effect from 18 November 2026, relinquishing his position as Chairman from the same date. At its meeting held on 9 November, the Board of Ex-pack resolved to appoint Thulci Aluwihare, an Independent, Non-Executive Director of the company, as Chairman of the Board with effect from 18 November 2026.

Kassim’s retirement on his 70th birthday marks the close of a distinguished chapter. A founding figure of Aberdeen Group, he played a central role in shaping the Group’s strategic direction and building it into the diversified business it is today. During his tenure as Chairman, he steered Ex-pack onto a path of sustained profitability, strengthening its financial foundations for the future. Under his leadership, Ex-pack also completed its Initial Public Offering and listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange, a significant milestone for both the company and the Group.

Aberdeen Group extends its deep appreciation to Kassim for his vision, guidance and steadfast commitment to Ex-pack, and for the strong foundation he leaves for the company’s next phase of growth.

title: Blue tsunami: American reformist revolution and new progressivism | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:28
-     - 48

Bernie Sanders and AOC ‘Fighting Oligarchy’ tour 2025 revived Democratic base

Some events act as a ‘tester’ of your determinant drives and motivating passions, manifested in spontaneous reflexes. I rejoiced at the Blue Tsunami (or ‘Blunami’ as American youngsters say) of the US Democrat victory in both Houses of Congress—though aware of the possible implications for Ukraine-Russia, and for Sri Lanka, of a much more liberal Congress. 

The Sri Lankan angle didn’t dampen my delight at the Democratic triumph because my core identity is as a human being and is therefore universalist, and I am convinced that on balance, this Democratic victory is also a victory more generally for humanity. I also think the Democrat tsunami provides a great example for Sri Lanka. 

When I emailed my old PhD supervisor and friend, Emeritus Professor John Kane, author of ‘Between Virtue and Power: The Persistent Moral Dilemma of US Foreign Policy’ (Yale University Press), about the Republican rout in both houses of Congress, he wrote back exultantly: “Can’t take my eyes away. It is much more devastating than even I’d hoped for!”.

As observed by CNN, come 3 January, 75% of the USA will be governed by the Democrats.

Social democratic populism

Sir Isaiah Berlin made a breakthrough in political discernment when he said that in politics we often have to make painful choices between desirable values or clusters of values. The three great ideals of the French Revolution—Liberty, Equality, Fraternity—are almost never available together in the real world. It is almost always a lacerating choice. I’d say we are lucky if any two of the three are together, but are luckiest when the three great values appear, however episodically or ephemerally, interlinked. 

The victory of this generation of US Democrats re-bundles the values of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity, even for a moment. 

The US mid-term election was a double revolution, a ‘revolution in the revolution’ (to echo Regis Debray). It was not only a victory over the right-wing, ultranationalist ruling Republican ideology and agenda of Donald Trump, but was also a seismic shift in the Opposition, within the US Democrats, away from the neoliberal, pro-war, pro-intervention, pro-Israeli paradigm of Hillary Clinton, towards the ideology and agenda of the Progressive Democrat Caucus chaired by Senator Bernie Sanders with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and the ‘Squad’ as prominent members. 

Secondarily, it also reflects the catalytic role of the Democratic Socialist Alliance (DSA) which has seven members in the new Congress making it the largest number of self-declared Socialists in the history of the US Congress.  

85-year-old Bernie Sanders inspired a peaceful revolutionary change in public consciousness by combining moral-ethical leadership with sharply analytical socioeconomic critique in his decades-long career and tireless campaigning over the last ten years, all over the United States. The winning Democratic candidates are ‘Bernie’s Children’, who could ‘Feel the Bern’ back in 2016. At that election the Democratic party establishment sabotaged Bernie Sanders and threw the nomination to neoliberal Hillary Clinton, though the New York Times had editorialised that the only one who could possibly defeat Trump that year was Bernie because he, unlike Hillary, epitomised change and had fired-up the enthusiasm of youth and blue-collar voters. Trump decisively beat Hillary.

After Trump’s dramatic 2024 comeback despite the subversive 6 January 2020 siege of the Congress, defeating Kamala Harris who paid the price of Joe Biden’s enabling of Netanyahu’s Gaza genocide, the Democrats were demoralised and disorganised. In a heroic gesture rare in modern democratic politics, Bernie Sanders began a lone speaking tour of the USA, and was almost immediately joined by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, leader of The Squad of young women who had waged an alternative campaign to beat the Democratic establishment, win party nominations and elections. AOC, a DSA member, was the youngest person ever to be elected to the US Congress. 


The multi-city, cross-country Bernie-AOC tour, billed ‘Fighting Oligarchy’, ran from February to April 2025. Drawing large crowds, it inspired the ‘No Kings’ protest movement of mid-2025 through to 2026. That was how the progressive mass movement of resistance to Trump was reignited, which revived, renovated and repositioned the Democratic party, shifting the tectonic plates of American consciousness and generating the Blue Tsunami.      

The open secret of the 2026 ‘Blue Tsunami’ is that the Democrats focused on economics—not in the sense of abstract macroeconomic statistics, but of the impact of economic policy on the lives and livelihoods of the common citizens, i.e. the “affordability” theme. The Democrats challenged the economic model pursued both by the Republicans and previous Democratic administrations, of the dominance of ‘the 1%’: the billionaires over the citizens. 

In the new Democratic slogans, we find the championing of “the Many over Money”. This is a progressive Populism within and compatible with liberal democracy and capitalism, but NOT neoliberal ‘free market fundamentalist’ capitalism, or simply ‘liberal capitalism’, to which it presents an alternative. The agenda of the Progressive Caucus has become the dominant discourse of the Democratic party and the winning wave. 

In the USA today, neoliberal economic doctrine has been rejected, with economic policies and models being assessed from the standpoint of outcome and impact; of material consequence: what they deliver to the people—whether they grind-down or uplift the majority of citizens. 

The ideology of the progressive Democrats, and even the pro-socialist agenda of the DSA-backed candidates, fall squarely within Social Democracy shared by Canada, Scandinavia, Spain, Brazil, Mexico, and UK Labour. 

The new progressivism could be defined as ‘populist Social Democracy’ or ‘Social Democratic populism’.    

The US, the birthplace of neoliberalism, was also the birthplace of a viable progressive counter to neoliberalism—not capitalism as such—by Nobel Prize-winners Joe Stiglitz and Paul Krugman and other renowned economists such as Robert Reich, Jeff Sachs and James Galbraith. 

Economic neoliberalism including ‘the Washington Consensus’ has now been discredited and dislodged in the metropolis, the citadel of world capitalism, and is sought to be replaced by a new pragmatic-progressive, people-centric economic philosophy from bottom-up.

While the proudest achievement of Trump was closing the borders to migration, his brutal exclusionary-nationalist gesture which should have reaped rich rewards Texas, especially along the bank of the Rio Grande which separates it from Mexico, didn’t decisively deliver votes. Moreover, in a stunning development, voters in conservative, rich Texas, pivoted against the massive AI data centers which have sprung up, consuming colossal amounts of water and threatening the ecology, and voted for progressive Democratic candidate James Talarico as Senator. He busted through an almost 40-year Republican fortress.      

Economic neoliberalism is being rejected throughout the Western hemisphere. Hundreds of thousands of students, workers and farmers in France, and a great many young people in Germany are demonstrating against the dominant economic doctrines that had made them and their families poorer while robbing them of the public services and educational facilities they had enjoyed. 

A major element of the Blue Tsunami is the victory of progressive Christianity/Christian progressivism over the colossally wealthy right-wing Evangelical variant. In his acceptance speech, the young Senator-elect from Texas, Harvard-educated James Talarico, a Presbyterian with a Master’s in Divinity who follows biblically-sourced Christian social teaching, said he entered politics inspired by Jesus Christ’s injunction to ‘love thy neighbour’. He denounces ‘Christian nationalism’, and hails Pope Francis and Pope Leo XIV as his heroes.    

In the fissure within Populism between on the one hand, Far-Right ultranationalism and on the other, Progressive Populism and Left Populism, the Far-Right ultranationalist Populist project has historically peaked and is in parabolic decline, from the defeat of Boris ‘Brexit’ Johnson through the (two) Bolsonaros and Netanyahu to the Trumpian Republicans. 

In Britain, the Conservatives and the Labour Right (Sir Keir Starmer) have been replaced by Manchester’s Andy Burnham whose hero is Neil Kinnock. Burnham has pledged to rebuild Britain’s public services and revive the economy’s public sector, rejecting ‘New Labour’ Tony Blair’s neoliberal economic roll-back of the State.    

US Republicans have begun to recoil from the Trumpian ultranationalist-militarist, pro-Netanyahu Right which doomed it to defeat and will probably bury it at the 2028 Presidential elections. JD Vance began the pushback. 

In France, Le Pen’s nationalist Right could win the presidency, but Jean-Luc Mélenchon is a viable Left candidate. His left bloc could prevail at the National Assembly elections, proving a powerful counterweight even if he loses the presidential race. 

America’s tectonic shift is an eye-opener for anyone but the most obdurate and ostrich-like: 

nBoth (a) economic neoliberalism and (b) ethnoreligious ultranationalism are in crisis and decline. 

nA new progressivism – social democratic populism—has won in the world’s leading power. As went New York City for Mamdani, so went the USA. 

Los Angeles has elected a Democratic mayor Nithya Raman, born in Kerala to a Tamil Brahmin family. She is America’s first woman mayor of South Asian origin. Both key mayors, Mamdani and Raman, are DSA-backed.

Netanyahu falling?

The Blue Tsunami broke the stranglehold of the hardline pro-Israeli AIPAC lobby over Jewish voters, Democratic voters and US politics. 72% of the Jewish vote went for Democrats. Senator-elect Dr Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan won a majority of Jewish votes despite his opposition to the Gaza genocide and support for Palestinian self-determination. 


In a rare favourable conjunction, the Democratic triumph came only days after Prime Minister Netanyahu was unable to win a majority in the Israeli election. The Netanyahu ‘brand’ and the Netanyahu-Trump axis no longer constitute a bridge but rather a wall between Israel and US voters. 

The US midterm revolt impacted Israel. Initially it was an impossible deadlock with General Gadi Eisenkot spurning backing from the Palestinian Arab MPs who formed a numerically strong group of 19 which held the balance. Netanyahu’s pressure and that of the smaller extremist Zionist parties lost its axiomatic veto-power when the Blue Tsunami made landfall. Post-midterm, Eisenkot did not rudely brush-off the Palestinian Arab parties’ offer of a safety-net. Therefore, he now has the written support of 67 MPs, tilting the balance. 

A former IDF Chief-of Staff whose son and nephews died in combat, Gadi Eisenkot is hardly a dove. He is author of the notorious Dahiya doctrine of disproportionate force against civilian infrastructure and areas. However, in their time, Menahem Begin, Yitzhak Rabin and Ariel Sharon were hawks but were persuaded into negotiated agreements and partial withdrawals by the US. The fall or retreat of Netanyahu and his religious-ultranationalist Government will end or pause the worst period in Israeli-Palestinian history, making possible a new equation with a Democratic administration in 2028 which can reopen negotiations with the Palestinians. 

An Eisenkot administration may reduce Zionist settler violence in the West Bank.  

Most crucially for the region and the world, a Democratic US President (2028) will return to some version of Obama’s JCPOA with Iran.

Lessons for Lankan politics

The Democratic tsunami provides an inspiration and model for the Sri Lankan citizenry and the Opposition. 

In the face of an arrogant President, the dramatic positive changes in the USA became possible only because the main Opposition party transformed. We don’t have mid-term elections in Sri Lanka and the Provincial Council elections which could function as such are nowhere on the horizon. Any positive change becomes possible only if the main Opposition party/parties – SJB, SLPP—change for the better and campaign differently. The US Democrats have shown how, so there is no excuse not to.

I have long expressed the view that a basic reason for the deep failures in Sri Lankan politics has been the absence of the equivalent of the US Democrats. Things weren’t always so. I grew up with a paternal generation from center-left to the left, whose consciousness was an eclectic mélange of Western culture, left-liberal democracy and Third Worldism: they were JFK fans, students of JK Galbraith’s economics, and sympathisers of US Democrats and UK Labour while admiring supporters of Nehru, Mao, Ho Chi Minh, Fidel Castro and Che Guevara. Within the UNP, Ranasinghe Premadasa was an explicitly Rooseveltian New Dealer and social democrat. 

With unipolarity segueing into the 21st century though, Sri Lankan politics was polarised between economic neoliberals and ultranationalist New Right, both identifying with the US Republicans, UK Conservatives, and even Israel’s Netanyahu, albeit for different reasons.  

SJB chief economist Dr Harsha de Silva recently commended the AKD Govt for ‘economic stabilisation’, adding the caveat ‘stability is not enough, jobs are also needed’, while by contrast the US Democrats are light-years ahead (as Premadasa was, starting with his 1973 April Rotary Club Colombo West address), critiquing and rejecting economic ‘stability’ which destabilises the economy of the vast majority of citizens, households, neighbourhoods and public services, as no meaningful, real ‘economic stability’ at all! 

The SJB criticizes the managerial inexperience and tactics of JVP-NPP economic policy but the US ‘Blue Tsunami’ criticizes the outcomes and logic of the dominant, billionaire-benefitting, citizen-impoverishing economic strategy and model.  

The ‘Blue Tsunami’ brings two intellectual-ideological-paradigmatic imperatives: 

1.That the SJB shift from its neoliberal ‘Economic Blueprint’ which catastrophically lost it the 2024 election, to the progressive economics of the US Democrats. 

2.That the SLPP, SLFP and allies shift from the 2019 deviation of Trump-Netanyahu ultranationalism, back to its progressive center-left roots and draw inspiration from Bernie Sanders, AOC and Mamdani.  

There is no realistic economic model for Sri Lanka beyond and better than the social democratic capitalist model which America’s progressive Democrats are articulating—and currently implementing successfully in New York City under Mayor Mamdani.

Sri Lanka had its precursor of the US Democrats 2025-2026 re-generation. Not yet 50, Ranasinghe Premadasa stepped away from Dudley Senanayake’s sluggish UNP in defeat in 1970, and facing a Government with a 2/3rds majority ruling under Emergency, launched a political movement called the Citizens’ Front (‘Puravesi Peramuna’) in 1972-1973. That catalysed and commenced the transformation of the UNP into the dynamic populist-democratic party of the 1977 ‘Green Tsunami’. 

With that legacy, and the current example of the US Democrats, the SJB has every reason not to restrict its political activity to Parliament, and to amend its ideology that has failed to seize the public imagination.   

‘Come Together’ (John Lennon) 

‘March separately, strike together’ advocated Trotsky. Civic organisations and Opposition parties from the SJB to the FSP dissented separately and resisted sequentially, delaying the PSTA and Organised Crime Bills. 

However, History shows that no single party can successfully resist and roll-back dictatorship. 

In 1921 Lenin introduced the United Front concept at the Communist International’s 3rd Congress. The 1930s Anti-Fascist Popular Front incorporated liberal democrats, defenders of a democratic republic but not necessarily socialism. In China and Vietnam, the Anti-Imperialist United Front included the ‘national bourgeoisie’, patriotic capitalists who valued national sovereignty and opposed foreign invasion/domination. 

The parents of the Anti-Fascist Alliance came from Left and Right. Churchill catapulted to the prime ministership from backbencher because he had insisted for the longest time that Hitlerite fascism was the greatest global danger and western democracies should unite not only with each other but also with Stalin’s USSR. 

Chile's dictator Pinochet held a referendum to extend his rule and was defeated by ‘a concert of parties’ (‘Concertacion’) from Socialists to Christian Democrats. Pushed onto the defensive, he called a presidential election, losing to the Socialist candidate of a Center-Left coalition. Dictatorship died.

title: The unethical Customs rewards system | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:26
-     - 29

A power intended to uphold the rule of law should not be exercised to confer undue benefits on the very officers entrusted with enforcing it. Such a practice creates an inherent conflict of interest, undermines institutional integrity, and risks making unethical conduct and corruption widespread in exercising the discretionary powers by such public officers.

The legislative provision that paved the way for this alarming arrangement was introduced into the Sri Lanka Customs Ordinance through the Customs (Amendment) Act, No. 83 of 1988, under the then UNP Government. This was in the aftermath of the radical economic liberalisation policy introduced by President J. R. Jayewardene in 1977, which opened the country’s economy and significantly relaxed import controls.

The relevant provision, as introduced, reads as follows:

“153. The amount--

(1) of all forfeitures and penalties recovered under this Ordinance or under this Ordinance read with the provisions of any other written law; and

(2) of the proceeds of all such goods as may be disposed of by the Director-General under section 162 of this Ordinance, or under this Ordinance read with the provisions of any other written law,

shall be paid into the hands of such Director-General and shall (after deducting any expenses incurred) be paid and applied as follows : -

(a) one half to the Deputy Secretary to the Treasury, out of which sixty per centum shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund and the balance forty per centum to the Customs Officers Management and Compensation Fund (hereinafter in this Ordinance referred to as “ the Fund”) ; and

(b) the other half into a reward fund under the control of the Director-General for distribution, in accordance with a scheme to be approved by the Minister, among customs officers concerned and informers.”

The financial implications of this provision are particularly alarming. Out of the aggregate amount recovered through penalties and forfeitures imposed on errant importers, together with the proceeds realised from the disposal of seized goods, 30% goes to the Treasury while 70% goes to Customs officers and informers.

This allocation comprises:

n 30% to the Consolidated Fund: 60% of the first half of the recoveries. (153(2)(a)).

n 20% to the Customs Officers Management and Compensation Fund: 40% of the first half. (153(2)(a))

n 50% to the Reward Fund: the remaining half, to be distributed among the Customs officers concerned and informers under a scheme approved by the Minister. (153(2)(b))

It should be emphasised that informers, where applicable, receive only a negligible portion of the 50% allocated to the Reward Fund. The overwhelming share of this allocation is therefore intended for the benefit of Customs officers directly.

A legal power intended to punish Customs offences and protect public revenue should never be used to financially benefit the very officers responsible for enforcing the law. When the rewards given to these officers exceed the revenue retained by the State, it is not just a legal anomaly but a serious misuse of public funds and a threat to the integrity of law enforcement.

A request for information was submitted to Sri Lanka Customs on  19 October 2026 under the Right to Information Act, No. 12 of 2016, seeking details of the total amounts of penalties and forfeitures collected during the years 2023, 2024 and 2025, together with a breakdown of the amounts distributed among Customs officers and remitted to the Treasury.

The request also sought clarification as to whether the relevant distribution scheme had received the approval of the Minister in charge, as expressly required under Section 153(2)(b) of the Customs Ordinance. This is particularly important because it has been alleged that the scheme is implemented without obtaining the Minister’s approval, as required by law.

In its response dated 3 November 2026, SLC, despite its reputation for operational efficiency, surprisingly requested a further 21 working days to provide information that should ordinarily be readily available in its possession. Upon receipt of the requested information, a detailed article, if warranted, will be published, supported by relevant facts and figures to shed further light on this matter.

Performance-based incentives v. penalties-based rewards

There is nothing wrong with public officers, particularly those responsible for collecting and protecting Government revenue, receiving reasonable performance-based incentives. However, such incentives should be based on clear annual targets and an objective assessment of each officer’s performance under a transparent scheme applicable equally to all staff. The incentive scheme of the Inland Revenue Department is a good example of this legitimate approach to staff management.

However, such a penalty-based reward system can give rise to several serious adverse consequences that deserve urgent attention from both the Government and the public. It must be emphasised that the concern is not directed at the Customs officers as a whole. Many officers perform their duties honestly and diligently. Unfortunately, the questionable conduct of a few can tarnish the reputation of the entire service, undermine public confidence and bring discredit to the many dedicated officers who uphold the integrity of the institution.

1. Conflict of interest

A conflict of interest arises when a public officer’s personal or financial interests may influence, or appear to influence, the proper performance of official duties. Public officers are expected to make decisions solely in the public interest and in accordance with the law, without being influenced by the prospect of personal financial benefits.

For example, when Customs officers are entitled to receive financial rewards from penalties and forfeitures imposed on importers, they may develop an indirect personal interest in detecting more offences and imposing higher penalties. This creates a situation where the officers responsible for investigating violations and enforcing the law may also benefit financially from the very penalties they impose.

The fundamental problem is that those entrusted with enforcing the law should not have a personal financial interest in the outcome of their own enforcement actions. Law enforcement must be guided by justice, fairness and the protection of public revenue, not by the financial rewards that may arise from punishing those who violate the law.

2. Erosion of public confidence

The public expects public officials, especially revenue officials such as Customs officers to enforce the law fairly and impartially, without being influenced by personal financial benefits. Importers should not have to worry about whether enforcement decisions are made in the interest of the law or financial gain.

When honest importers face unnecessary difficulties, excessive penalties or unofficial demands to clear their goods, they may lose confidence in the system and even resort to unlawful practices. Ultimately, this discourages tax compliance, undermines public confidence and results in losses to State revenue.

3. Harassment and disproportionate enforcement

Not every Customs violation involves an attempt to evade duties or defraud the State. Some may arise from genuine mistakes, differences in interpretation, documentation errors or technical non-compliance. Such cases should ordinarily be dealt with through additional duties, commonly known as Additional Estimates (AEs), where applicable, rather than punitive penalties and forfeitures that generate financial rewards for enforcement officers.

It is alleged that certain Customs officers take excessive personal interest in investigating and prosecuting importers, sometimes going beyond what is reasonably necessary to enforce the law. This raises concerns that the prospect of personal financial rewards may influence enforcement decisions, shifting the focus from justice and revenue protection to personal financial gain.

4. Compromising professional integrity

Customs officers should measure their performance by the quality of their investigations, accuracy of their decisions, fairness of enforcement and contribution to national revenue.

However, when financial rewards are linked to penalties, the focus may gradually shift from professional performance to the amount of money generated through enforcement activities. This can undermine the professional ethics and integrity expected of public officers.

5. Weakening the rule of law

The rule of law requires that laws be enforced fairly, consistently and without personal interests influencing official decisions.

An enforcement system should not encourage officers to view every violation as an opportunity to generate financial benefits. Penalties must be imposed according to the law and the seriousness of the offence, not according to the financial rewards they may produce. Otherwise, the distinction between enforcing the law and exploiting the law becomes dangerously dim.

6. Institutionalising a conflict of interest

Perhaps the most serious consequence is that such an arrangement can make a conflict of interest part of the institutional structure itself.

Normally, conflicts of interest are matters to be prevented through ethical standards, administrative controls and disciplinary procedures. But when legislation itself creates a financial entitlement for the officers responsible for imposing penalties, the problem becomes institutional rather than merely individual.

It may also become difficult to ensure independent analysis of enforcement decisions when the enforcing institution itself stands to benefit financially from those decisions.

Responsibility of the Government

Although the NPP Government has made considerable progress in combating political corruption, it has been less successful in eliminating bureaucratic corruption within the public service, particularly among revenue agencies that are entrusted with wide discretionary powers in the discharge of their official duties.

Revenue-collecting institutions such as Sri Lanka Customs fall within the direct purview of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, whose long-standing and vocal opposition to corruption has been a defining feature of his political career. Furthermore, the fact that his Secretary previously served as a senior officer of Sri Lanka Customs makes the need for meaningful intervention even more compelling.

It is therefore the solemn responsibility of this Government to take decisive action to eradicate corruption itself and its potential avenues within revenue-collecting institutions and restore public confidence in their integrity. This responsibility must not be compromised, weakened or diluted by resistance from vested interests, potentially corrupt elements within trade unions, or opportunistic opposition political forces seeking to obstruct genuine institutional reforms. The Government must demonstrate the political courage and determination to pursue these reforms in the public interest, particularly when no other foreseeable political force appears capable of undertaking such bold and necessary measures for the benefit of the nation and its people.

The fight against corruption cannot end with politicians; it must extend to every public institution and every public official entrusted with State power.

(The author is a Retired Deputy Commissioner General, Inland Revenue Department and could be reached via email mifly1234@gmail.com)

title: Twice promised, never delivered: Tax Ombudsman Sri Lanka still needs | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:25
-     - 37

Budget day is when the nation listens for numbers, revenue targets, new rates and new reliefs. Behind those numbers lies a quieter but equally important question. How fairly will the State collect the taxes that fill its coffers?

Over the past few years, Sri Lanka has tightened tax administration considerably, and rightly so. Revenue mobilisation has been central to our recovery. The Inland Revenue Department has expanded its use of data, third-party information, digital filing, risk-based audits and stronger enforcement.

But enforcement is only one side of the social contract. When the State’s powers to assess, audit, recover and penalise grow, the taxpayer’s ability to seek fair redress must grow with them. As the net tightens, the scales must stay balanced. That is the case for an independent Tax Ombudsman.

Power needs a counterweight

Tax laws give administrators wide discretion. They can issue assessments based on estimates, call for information, conduct audits, impose penalties and interest, and recover tax through coercive measures. Most officers use these powers professionally and in good faith. Still, every tax system, however well run, will sometimes see actions that fall short of what the law intends.

Around the world, these issues tend to follow familiar patterns:

None of these is necessarily a dispute about the law itself. They are about how the law is applied in practice, and that is where a dedicated avenue for redress adds the most value.

Gap in our current framework

Sri Lanka has formal dispute resolution mechanisms: administrative review within the Department, the Tax Appeals Commission and ultimately the courts. These deal with the amount of tax. They are legalistic, time-consuming and often expensive, and for a small business owner, a salaried employee or a pensioner they are usually out of reach.


More importantly, these forums are not designed for complaints about conduct and process. Unreasonable delays, procedural unfairness, failure to follow published guidelines and disproportionate recovery action are not “appealable” in the conventional sense. Yet these shape a taxpayer’s experience of the system and, with it, their willingness to comply.

The idea is not new to Sri Lanka. A Tax Ombudsman was appointed in 2005, but the office was abolished in 2008. Establishing the office was again proposed in Budget 2017 and in Budget 2023, but neither proposal has been implemented. The lesson is clear, an office without a statute behind it does not last.

Why this matters for revenue, not just fairness

Some may see a Tax Ombudsman as a luxury Sri Lanka cannot afford. I would argue the opposite.

Tax morale, a citizen’s intrinsic willingness to pay, is one of the most powerful and least costly drivers of revenue. The OECD’s work on tax morale highlights the role of trust between taxpayers and tax administrations in encouraging compliance. When taxpayers feel powerless against the administration, compliance becomes grudging and avoidance becomes rationalised.

A Tax Ombudsman also helps the administration itself. Recurring complaints expose weaknesses in systems and procedures. Seen this way, an Ombudsman is a quality-assurance mechanism, not an adversary of the Inland Revenue Department.

Many countries have recognised that strong tax administrations need equally strong safeguards. Pakistan, South Africa, the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia have all set up independent offices where taxpayers can raise complaints about how they are treated by the tax authorities. The models differ, but the principle is the same, an efficient administration and a protected taxpayer are not in conflict. They reinforce each other.

What a Sri Lankan Tax Ombudsman should look like

1. Independence. A statutory office should be established by way of an Act of Parliamemt, independent of the Inland Revenue Department, with secure tenure, its own budget and reporting to Parliament.

2. A clear mandate. Maladministration, including delays, procedural unfairness, refund delays and disproportionate recovery action, without duplicating the Tax Appeals Commission’s role on the merits of assessments.

3. Accessibility. A simple, digital and free complaint process. A taxpayer should not need a lawyer or consultant to be heard.

4. Teeth. Power to call for records, recommend remedial action and require a written response within set timelines.

5. Transparency. An annual report to Parliament on complaint trends and systemic issues, so individual grievances lead to institutional reform.

Data, digitalisation and trust

Tax administration is becoming increasingly data-driven. Third-party data, information exchange and integration with banking and other systems give the State unprecedented visibility into citizens’ financial lives. This is necessary, but it raises legitimate concerns about data privacy, accuracy and use.

When a taxpayer believes their data has been mishandled, or that an automated risk flag has unfairly targeted them, where do they go? An Ombudsman provides that outlet and helps ensure that digitalisation builds trust rather than erodes it.

Budget signal worth sending

Budgets are statements of intent as much as statements of numbers. Announcing a Tax Ombudsman alongside continued revenue reforms would send a powerful message: the State expects every citizen to pay their fair share, and every citizen can expect to be treated fairly in return.

Sri Lanka has asked much of its taxpayers, and many have responded. The next step is to build a system that taxpayers trust, not merely fear. A strong tax administration collects revenue. A fair one sustains it.

The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author in her personal capacity.

title: Budget 2027: Prayer for better life from nation that has endured much | Daily FT

Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:24

Beyond economic statistics and promises, the people of Sri Lanka are looking for a realistic Budget that restores hope, creates opportunities and makes everyday life less difficult.

Today, 12 November, 2026, Parliament will witness the presentation of the National Budget for 2027 by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in his capacity as Minister of Finance. It will be the Government’s third Budget, presented at a time when Sri Lanka is still struggling to translate macroeconomic stabilisation into tangible improvements in the lives of its people.

For millions of Sri Lankans, this is more than another annual exercise in presenting revenue estimates, expenditure allocations and development proposals. It is an occasion that carries a simple but deeply felt expectation: that the coming year will be less difficult than the years they have endured.

Perhaps this is best described as a prayer from the poverty-stricken majority of our population — a prayer for affordable food, decent employment, reasonable household incomes, accessible healthcare and education, and the opportunity to live with dignity rather than merely survive.

Sri Lanka has undoubtedly made progress since the unprecedented economic crisis of 2022. Economic growth has returned, inflation has been brought under control compared with the extraordinary levels experienced during the crisis, debt restructuring has been completed, and the IMF-supported program has helped restore a degree of international confidence.

These achievements should not be underestimated. However, stabilising the economy and restoring the quality of life of its citizens are two different challenges.

Uncomfortable reality

The uncomfortable reality is that many households continue to experience the consequences of the economic crisis. The cost of living remains a serious concern, purchasing power has not recovered adequately, poverty has increased, and the burden of taxation and essential expenditure continues to weigh heavily on working families. Young graduates struggle to find suitable employment, while many skilled and educated young people see migration as their only realistic opportunity for a better future.

Economic growth figures, however encouraging, mean little to a family that cannot comfortably afford three meals a day, a parent unable to meet a child’s educational expenses, or a young graduate unable to secure a meaningful job.

The poverty headcount index, which rose to 16% in the first quarter of 2025 from 14.3% in 2019, illustrates the human cost of the economic crisis. Furthermore, the substantial increase in the official poverty line demonstrates why poverty cannot be measured without taking account of the rising cost of maintaining a basic standard of living.

Growth must become meaningful to ordinary people

The Central Bank’s projection of economic growth within the 4%-5% range for 2026 offers some encouragement. Yet the important question is whether this growth is sustainable and capable of generating productive employment, higher real incomes and improved living standards.


A recovery driven largely by the statistical effects of an earlier contraction cannot, by itself, guarantee long-term prosperity. Sri Lanka needs a different quality of growth — growth supported by private investment, exports, agricultural productivity, technology, innovation and competitive industries.

This brings us to one of the country’s most pressing concerns: investor confidence.

Sri Lanka cannot expect to overcome its foreign exchange constraints and create sufficient employment without attracting substantial foreign and domestic investment. The uncertainty surrounding major investment proposals, including the proposed Sinopec refinery project in Hambantota, illustrates the importance of consistency, institutional coordination and timely decision-making.

An investor must have confidence that agreements reached with the Government will be honoured, policies will not change unpredictably and administrative procedures will not become unnecessary obstacles.

Investment is not simply about bringing foreign currency into the country. It creates employment, transfers technology, develops skills, expands exports and generates tax revenue. A country that wishes to provide better opportunities for its younger generation must become a country in which investors are confident about committing their capital.

A Budget is only as good as its implementation

Another important concern is the effectiveness of public expenditure. Allocating billions of rupees for development and welfare is not sufficient if the money remains unutilised or fails to reach its intended beneficiaries.

The reported slow utilisation of budgetary allocations, including funds intended for people affected by the Ditwah disaster, raises legitimate questions about administrative efficiency and accountability.

The public does not expect merely impressive budgetary announcements. It expects roads to be repaired, schools to be improved, hospitals to receive essential facilities, disaster-affected families to be assisted and development projects to be completed on time.

The Government must therefore recognise that public administration is as important as public finance. Greater coordination between ministries, transparent procurement, digitalisation, clear institutional
responsibilities and measurable performance targets are essential.

Equally important is responsible management of State-owned enterprises. Public resources should not be continuously committed to commercially unviable activities at the expense of education, healthcare, social protection and essential infrastructure. Private enterprise should be encouraged to compete and invest wherever appropriate, while the State concentrates on effective regulation, essential public services and protecting vulnerable citizens.

What should the people reasonably expect?

The people are not asking for unrealistic subsidies or benefits that the national economy cannot afford. They understand that Sri Lanka has limited fiscal space, substantial debt obligations and continuing external vulnerabilities.

What they reasonably expect is a Budget that demonstrates fairness, discipline and compassion.

It should prioritise targeted assistance for genuinely vulnerable households, rather than politically attractive but economically unsustainable concessions. It should create an environment for private investment and employment, reduce unnecessary barriers to business, strengthen vocational and technical education, improve agricultural productivity and expand opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises.

It should also address the heavy burden placed on the formal working population and ensure that taxation is fair, predictable and supportive of productive economic activity.

Above all, the Government should establish a credible framework for translating budgetary promises into measurable results. Citizens deserve to know not only how much money has been allocated, but also what has actually been achieved with it.

Beyond 12 November: Restoring hope

It would be unrealistic to expect a single Budget to resolve all the structural problems that have accumulated over decades. Nor should anyone imagine that the Budget speech delivered today will immediately change the circumstances of millions of struggling families.

Indeed, the Budget has already been prepared. Nevertheless, the first reading of the 2027 Budget provides an appropriate occasion to remind the country’s leadership of the expectations, anxieties and aspirations of the people on whose behalf public finances are managed.

The Government’s vision of creating a prosperous nation and a beautiful life must ultimately be judged by the everyday experiences of its citizens. Prosperity cannot be confined to national accounts, investment announcements or economic growth percentages. It must be reflected in a family’s ability to meet its monthly expenses, a young person’s ability to find employment, a farmer’s ability to earn a reasonable income and an elderly person’s ability to live without financial insecurity.

Sri Lanka has paid an extraordinarily high price for years of economic mismanagement, institutional weaknesses and policy inconsistency. Its people have made painful sacrifices. They deserve an economic future that does not demand endless sacrifice without delivering meaningful rewards.

As the President presents Budget 2027, the hope of the nation is therefore neither extravagant nor unreasonable. It is simply that the coming year will bring fewer hardships, greater opportunities, fairer economic conditions and renewed confidence in tomorrow.

Ultimately, the success of Budget 2027 should not be measured by how impressively it is presented in Parliament, but by how much easier it makes life for the ordinary people of Sri Lanka.

That is the prayer of the people. And that is the responsibility of those entrusted with governing the country.

title: 2027 Budget: Need to revisit APIT | Daily FT
summary:
