There is a fundamental principle that deserves greater consideration when determining the taxation of employment income.

A salary is the remuneration an individual receives in return for services rendered. It represents the agreed compensation for the employee’s time, knowledge, skills, experience, responsibilities and contribution to the organisation. An employee earns what he or she receives through the service provided. The amount of remuneration may differ according to professional qualifications, experience, the nature of responsibilities and the value attached to the service. However, the fundamental character of that income remains the same. It is remuneration earned through employment.

Why should the nature and tax treatment of such earnings be progressively altered merely because the amount of remuneration is higher?

Recognising differences in salaries is one thing; using those differences as the sole basis for progressively changing the tax treatment of employment remuneration is another. The argument is not that all employees should receive equal salaries or that higher earnings should be exempt from taxation. It is that remuneration earned through employment should be recognised as a distinct category of income and subjected to a consistent and predictable tax principle. The fact that an individual earns a higher salary does not change the fundamental nature of that income as remuneration for services rendered. This distinction deserves recognition in the design of a fair taxation system.

Practical alternative: Uniform rate for employment income

In the light of these considerations, I propose that employment income be treated as a distinct category for personal income taxation, with a simpler and more predictable method of assessment. The proposed arrangement would rest on three basic principles:

Income from investments, rental properties, business activities and other sources could continue to be assessed under the relevant tax provisions, with appropriate safeguards to ensure that the common tax-free allowance is not duplicated.


Such an arrangement would introduce greater simplicity and predictability into the taxation of employment income. It would also prevent an employee’s remuneration from being pushed into a higher marginal tax bracket merely because the individual happens to receive additional income from another source. The proposal does not seek to exempt employees from their responsibility to contribute to public revenue. On the contrary, it seeks to establish a more rational and transparent method of determining that contribution. The appropriate uniform rate would, of course, need to be determined after careful fiscal analysis, taking account of revenue requirements, distributional consequences and the overall tax structure.

Taxation must encourage productivity, not discourage it

Another important consideration is the relationship between taxation and economic growth.

Sri Lanka is undergoing a demanding economic adjustment process. The continuation of economic reforms requires public confidence, private investment, increased exports, employment generation and the expansion of productive economic activity. It is important to recognise that households have already experienced considerable pressure through higher living costs and taxation. 

The sustainability of economic reforms cannot be secured through fiscal consolidation alone. There must also be visible progress in creating economic opportunities, expanding production, attracting investment and improving the earning capacity of the population. A tax system that is perceived as unreasonable or unpredictable can weaken public confidence and discourage individuals from undertaking additional productive activities. The objective should therefore be to broaden the revenue base through economic expansion rather than rely excessively on increasing the burden on existing taxpayers.

Borrowing, expenditure and fiscal responsibility

The question of taxation cannot be considered in isolation from Government expenditure and borrowing.

Borrowing may be necessary for a country facing extraordinary economic circumstances. However, it cannot become a permanent substitute for sound revenue management or a means of financing unlimited expenditure.

Equally important is the quality and productivity of public expenditure. Borrowed funds and tax revenue should be directed towards activities that strengthen the economy, improve productive capacity and generate sustainable returns. Fiscal discipline must therefore be accompanied by expenditure discipline, transparency and accountability. The public is entitled to expect that the sacrifices demanded through taxation will be matched by responsible management of public resources.

A timely appeal ahead of the Budget

As the Government prepares to present the 2027 Budget, there is an opportunity to reconsider certain aspects of the existing taxation framework. The purpose of this appeal is not to question the Government’s legitimate need to raise revenue or to undermine the economic reform program. It is to encourage a more balanced and equitable approach to achieving those objectives.

A taxation system must command public acceptance not merely because it is imposed by law, but because the principles underlying it are reasonable and defensible. The proposed separate treatment of employment income, with a common tax-free threshold followed by a uniform rate, is one such reform deserving serious consideration.

A good Budget is not measured solely by the amount of revenue it collects, but also by the fairness of the methods through which that revenue is raised and the economic value generated by its expenditure. The ultimate objective of taxation should be to strengthen the State without weakening the people and the productive economy that sustain it.

title: We opened the door to trade first. Then we stood still | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:22
-     - 28

In 1977, Sri Lanka was among the developing world’s pioneers in open trade and outward orientation. Viet Nam and Bangladesh followed much later, yet both have since moved far ahead. Understanding why matters if Sri Lanka is to recover the promise of those early reforms

In 1977, Sri Lanka took a bold step. At a time when most developing Asia remained suspicious of international markets, Sri Lanka dismantled import controls, unified the exchange rate, welcomed foreign investors and established the Greater Colombo Economic Commission, including the country’s first export processing zone at Katunayake.

The response was immediate. Exports, which had contracted during the closed-economy years of the early 1970s, rose to around 30% of GDP by the early 1980s. Sri Lanka briefly became an example to the developing world: a small island prepared to earn its place in the global economy.

Almost half a century later, an uncomfortable question remains. If Sri Lanka opened its economy first, how did it fall so far behind?

 The contrast is shocking. In 1990, Sri Lanka, Viet Nam and Bangladesh each exported roughly $2 billion in goods annually. Viet Nam was a war-scarred, centrally planned economy only four years into its Doi Moi reforms. Bangladesh was among the poorest countries in the world. Sri Lanka, by comparison, had a thirteen-year head start, a highly literate workforce and a position beside one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes.

By 2025, Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports had reached about $13.6 billion. Including services, total export earnings stood at a record $17.3 billion. That is an achievement, but the comparison with our competitors is disheartening. Bangladesh shipped goods worth $48.3 billion in its latest fiscal year, about three and a half times Sri Lanka’s total. Viet Nam exported $473 billion, roughly 35 times our figure. Its electronics exports alone, worth $106 billion, were nearly eight times the value of all Sri Lankan merchandise exports.

 Merchandise exports, 1990 and 2025 ($ billion).

The more troubling comparison is not with Viet Nam or Bangladesh, but with Sri Lanka’s own past. In 2000, exports amounted to one-third of GDP. By 2021, goods exports had fallen below 15%, approaching the levels seen during the inward-looking early 1970s that the 1977 reforms were intended to leave behind.

The economy continued to expand, but growth increasingly relied on borrowing, construction, and domestic consumption rather than income earned abroad. The consequences were painfully clear in 2022, when Sri Lanka ran out of foreign currency to pay for fuel, medicine, and food.

How did this happen?

The problem was not openness or outward-orientation itself. Every economy that has moved from poverty to prosperity without relying on oil or mineral wealth, including Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia and, more recently, Viet Nam, has done so through exports. A country of 22 million people cannot become prosperous by selling mainly to its own consumers.

The new policy was good. What failed was Sri Lanka’s ability to sustain it.

Sri Lanka stopped reforming. Vietnam and Bangladesh began later, but they continued. Sri Lanka’s liberalisation lost momentum and eventually reversed. Successive Governments introduced para-tariffs such as CESS and the Ports and Airports Development Levy. These measures raised revenue and protected favored industries while creating an anti-export bias.

According to the World Bank, Sri Lanka’s simple average import duty is about 19%, including para-tariffs that account for 11%age points. Import taxes also act as taxes on exports. They increase the cost of machinery, fabric and components used by exporters, while making the protected domestic market more attractive than the far more demanding international one. 

Sri Lanka also remained largely outside global value chains. Modern trade rarely involves producing an entire product within one country. It is built around specialised tasks performed across networks of factories, suppliers and markets in several countries.

Viet Nam understood this shift. It actively attracted multinational manufacturers, entered trade agreements with Europe, its Pacific partners and neighboring Asian economies, and made itself one of the region’s most attractive locations for electronics assembly. Foreign-invested companies now account for about 77% of Viet Nam’s exports.

Sri Lanka attracted too little foreign investment directed towards exports. It entered relatively few trade agreements outside South Asia and continued to depend heavily on garments, tea and rubber, much as it had a generation earlier.

Sri Lanka’s export base remained narrow. For decades after independence, tea, rubber and coconut supplied much of the country’s export income. Their prices were volatile and tended to decline relative to the cost of the goods Sri Lanka needed to import.

Garments eventually widened the export base, but much of the subsequent growth came from selling larger quantities of familiar products rather than developing successful new ones. Exporters experimented with hundreds of products, but few achieved lasting commercial success. At the same time, factories imported much of the fabric, machinery, and other components they used. A significant portion of each export dollar therefore flowed back out of the country, limiting the value retained at home.

Foreign investors were often kept at a distance by a complicated tax system, unpredictable regulation, and expensive logistics. Although successive Governments periodically promoted FDI, creating an investment-friendly environment or investment facilitation was not on the agenda. Governments forgot that export-oriented foreign investment brings technology, management expertise, production knowledge, and access to international markets. By failing to attract enough FDI and retain foreign companies, Sri Lanka missed several benefits at once.

Trade relationships were also limited. Competitors entered deep, reciprocal agreements across Asia and with Europe. Sri Lanka concluded only one agreement outside South Asia (Thailand). Most of them, if not all, were ineffective. Even the free trade agreement with India remained underused and unbalanced. Most Governments feared opening to such relationships. Even if Governments were in favor of free trade agreements, such initiatives were strongly opposed by self-interested political parties. Instead, exporters relied heavily on one-way preferences such as the European Union’s GSP+. These arrangements are useful, but they are conditional and can be withdrawn, as Sri Lanka discovered between 2010 and 2017.

Most importantly, Sri Lanka never developed a durable national trade agenda. In Viet Nam and Bangladesh, export growth became a national undertaking that survived changes in political leadership. In Sri Lanka, trade was often portrayed as a threat to employment, farmers, and national sovereignty, rather than as a means of creating more productive and better-paid jobs. Without broad public support, reform remained politically vulnerable. For Governments, introducing another levy was easier than making the case for competition and an open market.

True that Sri Lanka did face exceptional shocks: three decades of war, a tsunami, a pandemic and a sovereign default. These events undoubtedly held the country back. But war alone cannot explain why the decline continued after 2009, when peace created the best economic opportunity Sri Lanka had seen in a generation.


Behind all these failures lies a deeper reason. Sri Lanka has never had a national trade policy that was actually in force: a single framework, backed by all parties, that sets the direction of trade and holds every other instrument to it. Without such a policy, tariffs followed the Treasury’s revenue needs, trade agreements were pursued or shelved by whichever ministry held the file, and export and investment promotion each ran on separate plans. 

However, the Government attempted to formulate and implement a National Trade Policy in 2017. Although a policy was formulated and approved by the Cabinet, it was never turned into a time-bound action plan; the ministry responsible for it was restructured, and it quietly disappeared. It rested on three pillars: competitiveness through domestic reform, wider market access through a strategic program of trade agreements with both Asian and Western markets, and trade facilitation. Its first principle was predictability, consistency, and transparency. This framework can be revived, taking into account new developments at both national and global levels. Global value chains are being redrawn as firms spread production beyond China and closer to trusted markets. Services and digital trade account for a growing share of value, even inside manufactured goods. Sustainability standards increasingly decide who gets access to rich-country markets. A modern trade policy must treat these shifts as opportunities: positioning Sri Lanka as a reliable link in Asian value chains, letting producers import inputs freely, and turning standards and certification from a barrier into a source of competitiveness.

The gap matters even more today. The National Tariff Policy is a welcome step, but a tariff policy is an instrument, not a strategy. It cannot decide which trade agreements Sri Lanka should pursue, how to secure membership of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), how to respond when the United States changes its tariffs on our goods, or how exporters will meet Europe’s new carbon and deforestation rules. After all, trade policy goes beyond tariffs and encompasses a spectrum of instruments: WTO agreements, regional and bilateral agreements, trade facilitation, GVCs, the trade-FDI nexus, trade-related legal and regulatory measures, and coherence with macroeconomic policies, which are interconnected. Unfortunately, many, including those who advise Governments, think trade policy is just revisions to the import tariff structure.  

The National Tariff Policy proposes a simpler four-band structure of 0, 10, 20 and 30%. The Government has committed to eliminating CESS and the Ports and Airports Development Levy, with the phased removal of CESS due to begin in 2028. The World Bank estimates that removing para-tariffs could increase household consumption by an average of 3.1%, with the poorest households receiving the greatest gains. A National Export Development Plan for 2026 to 2030 has also been prepared, and exporters’ associations have supported the reforms. But without a national trade policy above them, these remain separate instruments, vulnerable to the next budget or the next change of Government.

This paper ends with a straightforward proposal. Sri Lanka should adopt a national trade policy and a trade development strategy, agreed across party lines and endorsed by Parliament, to guide the National Tariff Policy, trade agreements, investment promotion and the export plan alike. It should have an owner: a properly staffed trade agency working through an inter-ministerial council, with the policy reviewed every three years. 

(The author is an international trade specialist, a former United Nations Director of Trade and Investment, and former Chief Economist for the Asia-Pacific region at ESCAP)

title: Five initiatives, eight capitals, one vision for Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 12 November 2026 00:20
-     - 28

Introduction

The current NPP Government will present its third Budget to Parliament on 12 November 2026. Among citizens’ many expectations, the Government also aims to deliver on its election manifesto commitments in this Budget. It will allocate the necessary funds to continue initiatives already underway since 2024. In my view, five national initiatives share overlapping sustainable development objectives, including building a prosperous, inclusive, and sustainable nation. These are: (1) A Thriving Nation – A Beautiful Life (the NPP Government’s election manifesto), (2) Digital Economy, (3) Prajashakthi, (4) Clean Sri Lanka, and (5) the work of the Sustainable Development Council (SDC). The last is not a national-level initiative; however, it measures the country’s overall performance in development activities. These initiatives have distinct mandates and implementation mechanisms. However, they share a common aspiration from NPP’s Election Manifesto: to enhance people’s quality of life and well-being through economic progress, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and good governance. 

One might ask whether the new Budget brings new development projects. Whatever the outcome of the Budget proposals, the central question one should ask is not whether Sri Lanka needs more development initiatives, but how existing initiatives can be integrated into a coherent national development framework that delivers measurable benefits to communities, as the market and the state have not addressed the salient problems facing the community-the third pillar. Rajan, Raghuram G. (2019), in his book titled “The Third Pillar: How Markets and the State Leave the Community Behind”, argues that the state and markets have left communities behind.. The best option for aligning these three pillars is inclusive localism. This article shows how existing initiatives can be integrated into a coherent national development framework that delivers measurable community benefits.

Shared national goals, fragmented implementation

The NPP election manifesto, A Thriving Nation, sets out the overarching vision for economic and social transformation, or renaissance. The Digital Economy initiative promotes productivity, economic growth and development through technological innovation, digital infrastructure, and efficient public services. Prajashakthi focuses on reducing poverty, empowering communities, and supporting local economic development through Community Development Councils (CDCs) nationwide. Clean Sri Lanka emphasises environmental sustainability, ethical behaviour, civic responsibility, and social transformation. Meanwhile, the Sustainable Development Council, established under the Sustainable Development Act of 2017, promotes policy coherence and progress towards the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The SDGs have 17 goals, 169 targets and 234 unique global indicators. The Government initiatives mentioned above complement rather than compete with one another. However, without effective coordination, overlapping objectives may lead to duplicated activities, fragmented resource allocation, and missed opportunities for collaboration. The question then is how to integrate goals, funding allocation, monitoring and evaluation across all initiatives into a single framework while respecting original mandates. The next section will answer this question.

Eight capitals: The seeds of sustainable economic growth

Sri Lanka’s economy has grown at an annual rate of 4.5% since independence. This is the long-term growth rate, or structural rate of growth. Last year’s economic growth was 5%, slightly above the historical growth rate. The country has achieved many remarkable achievements in many areas except economic growth. To build a thriving nation and improve lives, higher per capita income is vital because Sri Lanka’s standard of living and well-being depend on the country’s ability to produce goods and services and increase income. However, according to SDC, the weakest area among all the 17 SDGs is decent economic growth. Economic growth and sustainable development do not occur in isolation. They depend on a nation’s capacity to develop, mobilise, and use its resources productively. Conventional economic analysis has emphasised investment in labour, human capital, physical capital, natural capital, and technological progress as major drivers of growth. 


Jean Tirole, a winner of the 2014 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, argues in his 2017 book, “Economics for the Common Good: Delve into Economics With A Nobel Prize Winner”, that economists have too much to learn from the social sciences and humanities. Andrew Leight, in his book How Economics Explains the World, beautifully explains how economic change has shaped the course of history. Economics helps us trace humanity’s progress from hunter-gatherer societies to the modern global economy. The Agricultural Revolution allowed for food surpluses and specialisation, and the Age of Sail, which facilitated global trade and colonisation, shaped the course of history. The Industrial Revolution marked a turning point, dramatically improving living standards through technological innovations. The World Wars and subsequent economic theories shaped 20th-century policies, leading to periods of prosperity but also inequality. Throughout, geography, culture, technology, and institutions played crucial roles in determining economic success. 

Many scholars argue that investing in conventional capital formation alone will not enrich community-level sustainability because the vulnerabilities and poverty communities face are multifaceted. Institutional economists such as Acemoglu, Robinson, and North stress that institutions shape economic development and material well-being. Adam Smith introduced the original economic conception of capital in 1777. Later, as the concept of capital broadened beyond its conventional economic meaning, sociologists also examined different forms of capital to enhance communities’ social well-being. These include cultural, economic, and social capital, as introduced by Pierre Bourdieu. James Coleman introduced social capital theory, while Lyda Judson Hanifan was among the earliest scholars to use the term. They used the notion of social capital in the context of community relationships and collective action. Amartya Sen’s foundational contributions include welfare economics, the capability approach to human development, social choice theory, and poverty analysis. Elinor Ostrom’s work on collective action and common-pool resource governance, as well as Robert David Putnam’s work on civic participation and social capital, are also particularly relevant to community development.

Political Economy uses three pillars—state, market, and community—to describe any country’s economic system. The market is an effective way to organise economic activity and drives innovation. Economics and politics are closely intertwined. The market has market failures, and the Government has Government failures, and both need each other to function properly. This does not mean the community should be ignored; the three pillars must be delicately balanced. In these circumstances, growth and sustainable development require a comprehensive understanding of the resource allocation and capabilities that underpin a nation’s long-term prosperity. Evaluating all perspectives mentioned above, the writer proposes the Integrated Eight-Capital Framework (IECF), which identifies eight interconnected foundations of growth and sustainable development: human, physical, natural, economic, social, cultural, institutional, and technological capitals. For details on the IECF, see the article published on 8 June, 2026[1].

These capitals are not unrelated or independent resources; they reinforce one another and collectively shape a nation’s ability to produce goods and services, build resilience, and support well-being. The IECF can be understood as the seeds of economic growth and sustainable development. Just as seeds require suitable conditions to grow, Government and the private sector should invest continuously in the formation of these capitals. Effective institutions, scientific knowledge, and community participation are needed to deliver lasting economic and social benefits. In fact, institutional capital can serve as a catalyst for capital. 

For example, environmental conservation protects natural capital, and effective public institutions create the conditions for productive investment. Social trust, cultural values, and community cooperation facilitate collective action and enhance the effectiveness of development programmes. Investment in education and health strengthens human capital, while digital infrastructure and innovation enhance technological capital. 

From this perspective, the forthcoming Budget should not be regarded simply as an annual statement of Government expenditure and revenue. It should also be viewed as a strategic instrument for developing the country’s eight capitals. This framework does not essentially require higher public expenditure. Instead, it demands more effective coordination, allocation, and evaluation of available resources. Public investment by the Government should be assessed by its contribution to capital formation, productivity, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and long-term development outcomes.

Sri Lanka’s five national initiatives present an opportunity to adopt an integrated approach. By aligning their shared objectives with the Eight-Capital Framework, the Government could establish a common basis for planning, Budgeting, implementation, and monitoring. The fundamental question for the national Budget should therefore be: How effectively will public resources be allocated to strengthen the eight capitals underpinning Sri Lanka’s sustainable economic growth and development?

Five initiatives relate to the eight capitals. Clean Sri Lanka links cultural, natural, social and institutional capital. A Thriving Nation-Beautiful Life links all eight capitals. Digital Economy addresses technology, institutional, human and economic capitals, while Prajashakthi links to economic, institutional, human and social capital. SDC provides institutional capital and monitors across all eight capitals.

Budget as an investment instrument: Capital-based Budgeting

Normally, a Budget has two expenditure components: current expenditure and capital expenditure. If the Government allocates funds for investment that strengthens capital, one can claim the Budget is capital-based or development-oriented. A Budget proposal should also include measurable returns or quantifiable indicators for performance appraisal.

In this context, the writer would introduce Integrated Eight-Capital Budgeting (IECB) as an analytical framework. Under this framework, the Government could classify its development expenditure by the primary capital it strengthens, identify secondary capital benefits, and set measurable indicators for expected outcomes. 

For example, investment in irrigation infrastructure would primarily strengthen physical capital, but could also improve natural capital through better water management, economic capital through increased agricultural productivity, and social capital through collective irrigation governance. This approach would help policymakers understand the broader developmental returns on public investment. The writer does not suggest that IECF replace prevailing systems of Government accounting, Budgeting, or fiscal reporting. Instead, it should supplement them by introducing a development-oriented perspective into Government resource allocation, monitoring, and evaluation.

Conclusion and way forward

The success of the five initiatives mentioned above depends on how far they have reached communities (third pillar). Inclusive localism matters for success; therefore, two important questions remain: first, how far those five initiatives have reached the community despite the fact that implementation of those initiatives has been completed for at least one year; the second question is how far our public sector workers, including field officers attached to national-level Government services and sub-national-level Government entities, have gone or how often they have visited their respective fields or communities, despite the fact that Sri Lanka has the largest public sector in South and Southeast Asia. The Government faces the challenging task of using the public sector effectively for the country’s development.

From an economic perspective, our argument is particularly interesting because conventional growth models implemented in Sri Lanka so far emphasise labour, human capital, physical capital, natural capital, and technological progress. Our proposed IECF extends the analysis by explicitly incorporating economic, cultural, social, and institutional capitals. The IECF can be used as the seeds for growth and sustainable development at community, divisional, district, provincial and national levels to integrate the activities and funding of all five-level initiatives and beyond.

Building on its foundation in clinical waste management, EnCare has expanded into environmental engineering, bringing specialist waste services, recycling and resource recovery together through one trusted partner.

Sisili Hanaro EnCare (Pvt) Ltd received the National Bronze Award in the Large Category, Service Sector, at the CNCI Achiever of Industrial Excellence Awards 2026, organised by the Ceylon National Chamber of Industries (CNCI). The achievement marks an important milestone for a Sri Lankan company working in one of the country’s most demanding service sectors: the safe management of hazardous and specialised waste.

The award also draws attention to work that is often out of sight, yet essential to hospitals, industries and communities. Over more than a decade, EnCare has developed its services around the technical and regulatory demands of the waste it handles.

Built to Meet National Needs

EnCare was established as a joint venture between Sisili Projects Consortium and South Korea’s Hanaro Eng. Co. Ltd. Its clinical waste management operations were developed under a tripartite agreement involving the Ministry of Health, the Central Environmental Authority (CEA) and the Sisili Hanaro joint venture. The arrangement combined local knowledge with international engineering experience within a regulated operating framework.

EnCare commenced clinical waste management operations in early 2014, when major hospitals were dealing with substantial backlogs. With its pilot facility still under development, the company handled approximately 30,000 kg of accumulated clinical waste alongside daily service requirements. During the COVID-19 pandemic, its in-house engineering team designed and built an interim treatment line within two weeks to help keep essential operations running. These experiences shaped the operational discipline and engineering expertise that remain central to EnCare’s continued progress.

One Partner for Distinct Waste Streams

Today, EnCare provides clinical waste collection, treatment and disposal for hospitals, laboratories and clinics. Its door-to-door service extends sanitary and clinical waste collection to households, bringing a structured solution to waste that can be difficult to manage through conventional domestic disposal channels.

For industrial and commercial clients, the portfolio includes pharmaceutical and cosmetic waste, hazardous chemical waste and marine waste management, alongside certified secure destruction of confidential documents and data. EnCare also operates an established business-to-business e-waste service covering segregation, recycling and secure handling of discarded electronics. These services allow clients to address different waste requirements through a single provider without overlooking the controls each stream demands.

Driving Progress Towards a Circular Economy

Through its established Material Recovery Facility (MRF), EnCare collects, sorts and recycles plastic waste from business clients. Alongside its e-waste management services, these operations contribute to a circular economy by recovering valuable materials and returning them to productive use, reducing the volume of waste sent for disposal. This approach builds on EnCare’s core expertise in managing specialised waste streams.

Not all waste streams, however, are suitable for recycling. Clinical, pharmaceutical and hazardous chemical waste require controlled handling and where necessary, specialised treatment and disposal. EnCare’s integrated approach addresses both priorities, recovering resources wherever safe and practicable while ensuring that waste requiring specialised treatment is managed responsibly.

Recognition Built on Delivery

Compliance, traceability and service reliability remain central to EnCare’s operations. The company’s progress also rests from the experience of its engineering and operational teams and on sustained cooperation with regulatory authorities, public sector institutions, business partners and clients.

The National Bronze Award acknowledges how far that collective effort has brought EnCare. Its next chapter will be defined by the same practical challenge that shaped its beginnings: finding the right solution for each waste stream, whether that means safe treatment, secure destruction or recovering materials that still have value.

RAWALPINDI: Centuries from the bats of former captain Dhananjaya de Silva and present captain Kusal Mendis saw Sri Lanka make a terrific comeback in the first Test against Pakistan at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium here yesterday.

With Pakistan dominating the first two days by piling up a score of 434-9 declared, De Silva and Mendis took the limelight on the third day by sharing a record double century partnership for the fifth wicket to put Sri Lanka back in control as they ended the day brought forward again by bad light, strongly placed on 404-4, to trail by 30 runs.

Overnight pair Kamindu Mendis and de Silva started positively. De Silva was let off at first slip by Saud Shakeel on 40 and he made them suffer, stroking his way to his 14th Test century to remain unbeaten on 167 scored off 241 balls inclusive of 20 fours. He is only seven short of improving on his career best score of 173. He led the fight back, constructing a proper Test match innings by showing immense patience and going after only the deliveries which were there to be hit. It was a lesson in tempo, elegance and calmness and it was a class act.

Mohammad Abbas gave Pakistan hope with the wicket of Kamindu for 58 (131 balls, 8 fours), but the other Mendis, Sri Lanka's captain Kusal Mendis, joined de Silva and they blunted the Pakistani bowling attack. The pair has batted out exactly 60 overs and added 249 runs in the process eclipsing the previous highest for the wicket of 207 between Thilan Samaraweera and Tillakaratne Dilshan at Lahore in 2009. Both batsmen completed their hundreds - De Silva his 14th and Mendis his 11th. Babar Azam kept rotating his pacers around and Arafat Minhas bowled a long spell of left-arm spin, but they looked helpless on a wicket that was at its best for batting.

There were no chances offered in the afternoon session as the runs continued to flow at a brisk pace and Pakistan were made to toil hard in the field. Sri Lanka added 127 runs in the session off 30 overs without losing a wicket. While De Silva completed his century Mendis looked calm and composed throughout his innings. He brought up his century in the final session to remain unbeaten on 117 scored off 188 deliveries (10 fours, 4 sixes).

As things stand, Sri Lanka will fancy their chances of securing a decent lead to put Pakistan under pressure on the fifth day. With rain forecast for the afternoon today, the game seems to be headed towards a draw. But with Pakistan one cannot rule out a result.

A very unique day for Sri Lanka with incoming skipper Kusal Mendis and outgoing Captain Dhananjaya de Silva scoring centuries in a record double century partnership

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

Sri Lanka’s new Test Captain Kusal Mendis reached new heights in his illustrious cricket career by becoming the first player from his country to score a hundred on debut as Test Captain.

Mendis achieved this landmark on the third day of the first Test at Rawalpindi where he scored his 11th Test hundred to remain 117* by the close, putting his team within touching distance of Pakistan’s first innings total.

It was a very unique day for Sri Lanka that saw both the outgoing skipper Dhananjaya de Silva (167*) and the incoming skipper Mendis hitting centuries and adding a record 249* runs together to lift Sri Lanka from 155-4 to 404-4.  

Mendis is the third player to achieve this landmark this year. He joined Afghanistan’s Rahmat Shah – 105* & 51 against Bangladesh at Abu Dhabi on 9 October, and Zimbabwean Brian Bennett – 128 & 58 against Afghanistan at Sharjah on 5 November.

Mendis becomes the 37th player in the overall list that comprises 9 Captains from Australia, 6 from England, 3 from South Africa, 5 from India, 3 from West Indies, 4 from New Zealand, 4 from Zimbabwe, 1 from Bangladesh and 1 from Afghanistan.

Greg Chappell of Australia (123 & 109*) v West Indies at Brisbane, 1975 and Virat Kohli of India (115 & 141) v Australia at Adelaide in 2014 are the only two Captains to score a century in each innings of a Test on debut as Captain.

The highest individual score made by a player on debut as Test Captain is 367* by South Africa’s Wiann Mulder against Zimbabwe at Queen's SC, Bulawayo in July 2025.
